title: Senior
excerpt: In the US, a senior is a student in the final year of high school or university.
example: "As a senior he finally got the best room in the frat house."
text: In the American system senior comes after freshman, sophomore and junior. It is the year of graduation, prom and big parties. Other countries usually split the years differently.

title: Sensa
excerpt: Sensa is Dutch slang for sensation. Students say it when something exciting or crazy happens.
example: "What a sensa story," she shouted after his wild account of the night before.
text: You use it when something interesting happens, or when someone tells a story full of crazy twists. Basically the Dutch student version of being shook.

title: Serving
excerpt: Serving means someone pulls off a look, style or vibe really strongly.
example: "With those sunglasses and that long coat she was serving. Main character at the train station."
text: After serving there is often the style someone gives off. Like "serving looks" or "serving rich girl". The word comes from ballroom and drag culture. It is close to slay and ate.

title: Sexting
excerpt: Sexting is sending sexual messages, photos or videos through your phone or an app.
example: "They had been sexting for weeks before they met for the first time."
text: With sexting, consent and privacy matter most. Sharing someone's nudes without permission is a crime in the Netherlands. And remember that what you send can keep going around.

title: SG
excerpt: SG is short for shotgun. Among Dutch students, calling SG means you have to shotgun a drink yourself.
example: "SG!" he shouted, and immediately had to do his own shotgun.
text: Call shotgun yourself and you really have to do one: saying it is doing it, no exceptions. So think twice before you shout it at a party. A shotgun means punching a hole in a can and drinking it in seconds.

title: Shade
excerpt: Shade is putting someone down in a subtle way, without saying it directly.
example: "Nice dress, my grandma had one just like it." That was pure shade.
text: Throwing shade comes from the drag scene in New York. It is a sneaky jab wrapped up as a compliment or a joke. People who throw shade rarely admit it was meant to be mean.

title: Sharken
excerpt: Sharken (sharking) means stealing someone else's date, usually at a gala or datediner.
example: During the gala the sharken between the tables started pretty fast.
text: It mostly happens when you don't click with your own date, but do click with someone else's. Usually at a gala or datediner. Not the nicest move. But it makes for great stories the next day.

title: Shitposting
excerpt: Shitposting means posting weird, bad or chaotic stuff on purpose, just for fun.
example: "Our dispuut account is basically just shitposting now. Bad memes and blurry photos."
text: A shitpost can be a random meme, a deliberately terrible edit or a nonsense reply. It is about the joke, not the quality. You find lots of shitposting on spam accounts.

title: Shook
excerpt: Shook means shocked, surprised or really impressed.
example: "They broke up? After six years? I'm shook."
text: Shook is a casual, over-the-top way to show you are surprised. Often after gossip, big news or an unexpected plot twist. It comes from being shaken.

title: Shot
excerpt: A shot is a small glass of strong liquor that you drink in one or a few sips.
example: "One more round of shots and then we're really going home."
text: The size of a shot is different per country and bar. Because liquor is strong, a few shots add up fast. Dutch people often say shotje. A famous one is the Jägerbomb.

title: Shotgun a beer
excerpt: Shotgunning a beer means punching a hole in a can and drinking it in a few seconds.
example: "On three we both shotgun a beer. Whoever's last buys the next round."
text: You poke a hole near the bottom of the can, put your mouth on it and then pop the tab. The air makes the beer rush out super fast. It is a party ritual, but you get a lot of alcohol in very quickly.

title: Side quest
excerpt: A side quest is a random detour or task that has nothing to do with your actual plan.
example: "I just went to get bread. Three hours later I was at a house party in Utrecht. Big side quest."
text: Side quest comes from games, where it is an optional mission next to the main story. In real life it is anything you end up doing while you planned something else. Often those are the best stories of the night.

title: Simp
excerpt: A simp is someone who tries way too hard for the person they have a crush on, without getting anything back.
example: "He sent her flowers again even though she never texts back. Such a simp."
text: Simping means putting yourself last for your crush. Always available, always paying, liking everything. The word is mostly used to tease. Someone who simps hard is usually also down bad.

title: Situationship
excerpt: A situationship is something between dating and a relationship. More than casual, but without a label.
example: "We see each other every weekend, sleep over and go to parties together. But it's not a relationship." A typical situationship.
text: In a situationship you do things that belong to a relationship. But without agreements, labels or a future. That can be fine. Often one of the two wants more though. Then it is time for the DTR talk. The Dutch would call it a scharrel.

title: Sjaars
excerpt: A sjaars is a first-year student, often a new member of a student association or the newest person in a student house.
example: As a sjaars she still had to get used to all the abbreviations at her new association.
text: Every Dutch student starts as a sjaars. Older students will remind you of that a lot. Sjaarzen are often given small tasks, like getting the drinks. The British word is fresher, the American one freshman.

title: Skeer
excerpt: Skeer is Dutch slang for being broke.
example: "I'm really skeer this month," he sighed when he saw his bank account.
text: Most students know the feeling all too well. Rent is high and the money from DUO only goes so far. At the end of the month the whole house is skeer.

title: Slay
excerpt: Slay means doing something really well, or looking amazing and confident.
example: "She gave her first speech as praeses without any notes. Slay."
text: Slay comes from Black and queer culture and blew up through fashion, drag and social media. You say it as a compliment for a look or performance. It is close to ate and serving.

title: Slide into the DMs
excerpt: Sliding into someone's DMs means sending them a private message, usually to flirt.
example: "He saw her at the party, didn't dare to say anything and slid into her DMs the next day."
text: You make the first move online, often with someone you don't know well yet. Reacting to a story is a popular way. It doesn't always work. But sometimes something great starts like that.

title: Slow fade
excerpt: A slow fade is slowly having less and less contact with someone, instead of clearly ending it.
example: "First he texted every day, then every other day, now once a week. This is a slow fade."
text: Unlike ghosting, a slow fade happens step by step. Shorter replies, fewer plans and less effort. In the end the contact is just gone. Being clear is usually kinder.

title: Smoelen
excerpt: Smoelen is what Dutch students shout to make a group go quiet. Basically: shut up!
example: "Smoelen!" the praeses shouted before starting his speech.
text: "Smoel" is a rude word for mouth. You hear the shout mostly at student associations, right before something important gets announced. It is loud, it is rude and it works.

title: Snatched
excerpt: Snatched means someone looks extremely good and sharp.
example: "After two months at the gym and in that new dress, she looked snatched."
text: Snatched comes from drag, ballroom, beauty and fashion. It is often about a very polished look. Or a small waist. It is close to slay.

title: Sneaky link
excerpt: A sneaky link is someone you secretly see for something romantic or sexual, without others knowing.
example: "Nobody in the house knows, but he's been her sneaky link for weeks."
text: With a sneaky link you keep it secret from friends, a partner or everyone. It isn't a relationship and isn't presented as one. It is like a scharrel, but undercover.

title: Sober
excerpt: Sober means you haven't had any alcohol or drugs.
example: "I'm sober this month. Sparkling water for me."
text: Sober can be about one night, but also a lifestyle without alcohol. More and more students do a month without drinking. Whoever stays sober is often the designated driver. Dutch students call a sober night droog staan.

title: Sociëteit
excerpt: The sociëteit is the clubhouse where members of a Dutch student association meet for drinks and parties.
example: On Friday night the sociëteit filled up with members for the weekly borrel.
text: Big associations have their own sociëteit, often an old building in the city centre. Members come there to have drinks, hold meetings and party. Most students just call it the soos.

title: Soft launch
excerpt: A soft launch is showing something in a subtle way without announcing it, like a new partner.
example: "She posted two wine glasses and a guy's hand on the table. Definitely a soft launch."
text: With a soft launch you drop hints. A hand, a shoulder or a second plate, but no face or name. Everyone starts guessing. When you make it official later, that is a hard launch.

title: Soos
excerpt: Soos is short for sociëteit, the clubhouse of a Dutch student association.
example: "See you at the soos tonight?" she texted her dispuut.
text: Students use the short version just as often as the full word. The soos is where the borrels, parties and late nights happen. Expect cheap beer and sticky floors.

title: Sophomore
excerpt: In the US, a sophomore is a student in the second year of high school or university.
example: "As a sophomore she could finally pick a room instead of being assigned one."
text: In the American system sophomore comes after freshman and before junior. The word is also used for an artist's second album: the sophomore album.

title: Sorority
excerpt: A sorority is an American student association, traditionally for women.
example: "She joined a sorority during her exchange. Now she knows the whole Greek alphabet."
text: Like fraternities, sororities organise parties, charity, housing and an alumni network. They often have Greek letters as their name. The Dutch version is a women's student association or a dispuut.

title: Spa goud
excerpt: Spa goud (gold Spa) is a funny Dutch nickname for a beer.
example: "Another spa goud for me," he said, laughing at the bar.
text: Spa is a famous brand of mineral water. Spa blauw is still water, spa rood is sparkling. So spa goud, the golden one, must be beer. As innocent as water. Obviously.

title: Spam account
excerpt: A spam account is a second account where you post a lot without thinking, no perfect feed needed.
example: "My breakfast, my cat and ten photos of the sunset? That goes on my spam account."
text: A spam account is like a FinSta or alt account. The difference is that you post a lot, without any pressure. Usually only close friends follow it. It is often full of shitposting.

title: Spannie
excerpt: Spannie is Dutch slang for exciting. Short for "spannend".
example: "So spannie that you're finally going to a hospi!" her friend texted.
text: It pops up anywhere something is a bit more exciting than normal. A date, an exam result, a hospi. Said with lots of exclamation marks.

title: Spiegelen
excerpt: Spiegelen (mirroring) means agreeing with someone to drink exactly the same, to see who lasts longest.
example: They agreed to spiegelen all night: whatever one drank, the other drank too.
text: It is mostly done to see who gives up first. That person is the labo of the two. Heavyweights love it. Lightweights should stay far away.

title: Spijtknor
excerpt: A spijtknor (regret oink) is someone who regrets not joining a traditional corps student association.
example: "I'm actually a bit of a spijtknor," he admitted after seeing the photos.
text: Corps members call outsiders knor. A spijtknor is a knor who looks at the parties, the friendships and the traditions and wishes they had joined. It is never too late, they say. Well, sometimes it is.

title: Spoorknor
excerpt: A spoorknor (rail oink) is a non-corps student who travels by train.
example: As a spoorknor he took the burgerrups to his internship every day.
text: The term is used for someone outside the corps who commutes by train, instead of cycling around town. A double tease in one word. Dutch student slang is efficient like that.

title: Stalking
excerpt: In online slang, stalking means going through someone's profile and old posts very thoroughly.
example: "I stalked her Instagram all the way back to 2016. Accidentally liked a photo."
text: Online people often say it as a joke for innocent scrolling. But real stalking is something very different. That is repeated unwanted behaviour that makes someone feel unsafe. And that is a crime.

title: Stan
excerpt: A stan is an extremely devoted fan of an artist, celebrity or team.
example: "She bought tickets for every show of the tour and knows every lyric. A real Taylor Swift stan."
text: The word comes from the song "Stan" by Eminem, about an obsessive fan. Now you use it as a noun and a verb. Like "we stan". That means you fully support something.

title: Stiften
excerpt: Stiften is a made-up Dutch student game where the rules are invented on the spot to confuse everyone.
example: During stiften he invented a completely new rule on the spot, just to cause confusion.
text: The game has no fixed rules. They are made up as you go. The idea comes from a sketch by Jiskefet, a cult Dutch comedy show. If you are confused, you are playing it right. IYKYK.

title: Stitch
excerpt: A stitch is a TikTok feature that puts a clip of someone else's video at the start of your own.
example: "Someone stitched his video asking 'what is an anytimer?' and explained it perfectly."
text: Unlike a duet, the original video doesn't play next to yours. It comes first, then your reaction follows. People use stitches to react, add something or correct someone.

title: Storytime
excerpt: Storytime is a video where someone tells a personal story, usually funny or dramatic.
example: "Storytime: how I accidentally ended up at the wrong gala."
text: You mostly see storytimes on TikTok and YouTube. A good storytime builds up tension so you keep watching. It is often combined with a GRWM video.

title: Strepen
excerpt: Strepen is a tradition at some Dutch student associations where someone gets doused with beer or water as a punishment.
example: For breaking a rule he got gestreept during the borrel.
text: It mostly happens at some student associations, for example when someone breaks an unwritten rule, the mores. Wear clothes you don't love too much. Just in case.

title: Student
excerpt: A student is someone who studies at a university or university of applied sciences.
example: As a first-year student she still had to get used to the lecture schedule.
text: In the Netherlands you can study at a research university (wo) or a university of applied sciences (hbo). Students follow courses and earn credits, starting with the propedeuse in the first year. And they learn a whole new language, as this dictionary shows.

title: Student union
excerpt: A student union is an organisation that represents students and often runs clubs, events and facilities.
example: "The student union is hosting a quiz in the campus bar tonight."
text: What a student union does differs per country and university. In the UK it is often also a building with bars and clubs. In the Netherlands it is spread out over the student council, study associations and student associations.

title: Studentenhuis
excerpt: A studentenhuis is a shared student house in the Netherlands, where you live with a group of housemates.
example: In her studentenhuis she lived with four other students from different programmes.
text: Most Dutch students don't live on campus, but in a studentenhuis in the city. You get your own room and share the kitchen, bathroom and living room. To get a room you usually have to go hospiteren first. Some houses have their own traditions, like deur verdienen.

title: Studentenreisproduct
excerpt: The studentenreisproduct is the free public transport pass Dutch students get through DUO.
example: With her studentenreisproduct she travelled to her parents for free that weekend.
text: You apply for it through DUO. You choose free travel on weekdays or at weekends, with a discount the rest of the time. International students can sometimes get it too, depending on their situation. Worth checking.

title: Studententien
excerpt: A studententien (student ten) is a 5.5 on an exam: not great, but a pass.
example: "A studententien, but I passed," he said, relieved about his grade.
text: Dutch grades go from 1 to 10, and a 5.5 is the lowest pass. Not a high grade, but you get your credits. After a hard exam that feels like a perfect ten. Hence the name.

title: Studentenvereniging
excerpt: A studentenvereniging is a Dutch student association: a social club for students, with its own groups, clubhouse and traditions.
example: At her studentenvereniging she met more people in one year than in all her years of secondary school.
text: Members come from different programmes and universities. Most associations have their own sociëteit, disputen, jaarclubs and traditions. Some are huge and traditional, like the corps. Others are small and relaxed. It is a bit like an American frat or sorority, Dutch style.

title: Studentikoos
excerpt: Studentikoos means typical of student life. Like this dictionary.
example: "That's so studentikoos of you," she said when he did pre-drinks before the bar yet again.
text: Studentikoos is anything that feels typically student: the traditions, the jokes, the slang, the cheap beer. This whole dictionary is a great example. The short version is stuko.

title: Studievereniging
excerpt: A studievereniging is a Dutch study association for students of one specific programme.
example: Through her studievereniging she went on a study trip to Berlin.
text: A studievereniging organises lectures, trips, career events and borrels for its members. It is usually linked to your faculty. It is cheaper and more relaxed than a studentenvereniging. And a great way for internationals to meet Dutch classmates.

title: Study abroad
excerpt: Studying abroad means doing part of your studies in another country.
example: "Next semester I'm studying abroad in Lisbon. I'll probably learn more about beach bars than economics."
text: A stay abroad can last a few weeks, a semester or a whole year. Often through your university or Erasmus. You are then an exchange student. For lots of students it is an unforgettable experience.

title: Study buddy
excerpt: A study buddy is someone you study with regularly, so you keep each other motivated.
example: "Without my study buddy I would never have passed statistics."
text: With a study buddy studying is less lonely. You explain hard material to each other and keep each other on track. A good study buddy also knows when it is time for coffee.

title: Study session
excerpt: A study session is a planned block of studying, alone or with others.
example: "Study session in the library at ten. A well-deserved beer at three."
text: A study session can be about one exam, one chapter or just catching up. Studying together motivates lots of people. As long as it doesn't turn into just chatting.

title: Stufi
excerpt: Stufi is short for "studiefinanciering", the Dutch student finance you get from DUO.
example: "Has your stufi come in yet this month?" her housemate asked.
text: The money helps students pay for their studies and living costs. It is a mix of a grant and a loan, depending on the rules of your year. Payday is the day the whole house is suddenly in a good mood.

title: Stuko
excerpt: Stuko is short for studentikoos: typical of student life.
example: "What a stuko comment," she joked after his typical student joke.
text: Shortening the word for student culture is, of course, extremely student culture. So stuko is a great example of itself.

title: De super
excerpt: De super is what Dutch students call the supermarket.
example: "I'm just popping to the super for beer," he called from the doorway.
text: Dutch students do their groceries at the super almost every day, often just for tonight's dinner. Students also use super as a booster, like in "superchill". You'll get used to it.

title: Sus
excerpt: Sus is short for suspicious. Something or someone seems shady or untrustworthy.
example: "He says he went to bed early, but his coat was still at the bar at four. Sus."
text: The word already existed, but the game Among Us made it huge. There you have to guess who the traitor is. Now people say sus about anything that feels weird or shady.
